steps.title: Replacing values element-by-element with .map()
steps.lede: Every order in the SwiftDrop dataset carries a three-letter city code. .map() lets you swap each code for its full city name in one line.

blocks.text: `Series.map()` accepts a Python function that takes a single value and returns a single value, then applies it to every element of the Series. Define `def to_upper(code): return code.upper()` and call `orders["city_code"].map(to_upper)` — every city code in the column is uppercased in one pass.

`Series.map()` also accepts a **dict** or another **Series** as a mapping correspondence. `orders["city_code"].map({"LOS": "Lagos", "ABJ": "Abuja", "KAN": "Kano"})` replaces each three-letter code with its full city name — no loop, no conditional logic.

before.caption: orders — city_code column holds three-letter codes

annotations.text: Dict maps each code to its full city name
.map(city_lookup) substitutes every code in one call

blocks.change_summary: city_code column (LOS/ABJ/KAN) mapped to full city names (Lagos/Abuja/Kano) using a dict lookup.

steps.title: Running a custom function across rows or columns with .apply()
steps.lede: When you need logic that spans multiple columns — like labelling an order 'fast' or 'slow' based on its delivery time — .apply() runs your function once per row.

blocks.text: Suppose you want to label every SwiftDrop order "fast" or "slow" based on its delivery time, using a rule you write yourself. `Series.map()` works on one column at a time, but this rule needs to read `delivery_time_minutes` and write a new column — that's a row-level operation.

`DataFrame.apply()` applies an arbitrary function along an axis of the DataFrame, operating on each **column** by default (`axis=0`), or on each **row** when `axis=1`. Write `def label_speed(row): return 'slow' if row['delivery_time_minutes'] > 25 else 'fast'`, then `orders.apply(label_speed, axis=1)` runs it once per row and returns one label per order.

steps.title: Map substitution and apply — key takeaways
steps.lede: Two tools for element-wise transformation: .map() for value substitution, .apply() for custom row or column logic.

blocks.text: `Series.map()` substitutes values element-by-element using a function, a dict, or another Series — ideal for recoding categories like city codes. `DataFrame.apply()` runs an arbitrary function along an axis: column-by-column by default, or row-by-row with `axis=1`. Use `apply()` when the logic needs to read across multiple columns of the same row.

remediation_steps.title: How .map() substitutes values — with a function or a dict
remediation_steps.lede: .map() accepts either a Python function or a dict. When you pass a function it is called on every element; when you pass a dict each matching key is replaced by its value.

blocks.text: `Series.map()` accepts a Python function that takes a single value and returns a single value, then applies it to every element of the Series. Define `def to_upper(code): return code.upper()` and call `orders["city_code"].map(to_upper)` — every city code is uppercased in one pass, with no loop.

`Series.map()` also accepts a **dict** as a mapping correspondence. Every element whose value matches a key is replaced by the corresponding dict value; elements with no matching key become `NaN`. Pass `{"LOS": "Lagos", "ABJ": "Abuja", "KAN": "Kano"}` to replace three-letter city codes with full names in one call.

city_lookup = {"LOS": "Lagos", "ABJ": "Abuja", "KAN": "Kano"}
orders["city_name"] = orders["city_code"].map(city_lookup)
print(orders["city_name"].head(3))
# Lagos, Abuja, Kano

.map(dict) replaces every code in one call

remediation_steps.title: What axis=1 means for .apply()
remediation_steps.lede: The axis argument tells .apply() which direction to travel — down columns or across rows.

blocks.text: `DataFrame.apply()` applies an arbitrary function along an axis of the DataFrame, operating on each column by default (`axis=0`), or on each row when `axis=1`. With `axis=1`, the function receives one row at a time as a Series, so it can read any column of that row. The return value becomes one element in the result Series — one label per order, for example.

annotations.text: axis=0: function sees each column as a Series

after.code:
# axis=1: function receives one row at a time
def label_speed(row):
    return 'slow' if row['delivery_time_minutes'] > 25 else 'fast'

orders['speed_label'] = orders.apply(label_speed, axis=1)

annotations.text: axis=1: function sees each row — can read any column

blocks.change_summary: axis=0 passes each column to the function; axis=1 passes each row, enabling multi-column logic.

tiles.title: Grouping, Aggregating, and Reshaping with melt

steps.title: Split, apply, combine — groupby in three steps
steps.lede: To find the average delivery time per city, you don't filter and average three times. groupby does all three steps — split, apply, combine — in one call.

blocks.text: **Group by** refers to a process involving one or more of the following steps: splitting the data into groups based on some criteria, applying a function to each group independently, and combining the results into a data structure. For SwiftDrop orders, that means splitting every order into its city's group, applying "average" within each group, then combining the per-city averages into one result.

An **aggregation** is a groupby operation that reduces each group to a single summary value per column — for example, computing the sum of `order_value` within each city group. The result has one row per group, not one row per original order.

blocks.title: Split → Apply → Combine
blocks.alt_text: 8 order rows are split into three city groups (Lagos, Abuja, Kano). An aggregation function is applied inside each group. The per-group results are combined into one summary table with one row per city.

steps.title: groupby in practice
steps.lede: Watch groupby split orders by city and aggregate delivery times and order values.

steps.title: Calling groupby and choosing an aggregation
steps.lede: One call chains the grouping key with the aggregation method. You can compute one statistic or several at once.

blocks.text: Call `df.groupby(key)` then chain an aggregation method such as `.sum()` or `.mean()` on the DataFrame or a selected column. Use `.agg([...])` to compute several aggregations at once. By default, the group keys become the index of the result: `orders.groupby("city")["delivery_time_minutes"].mean()` returns one average per city with city names as the index; `orders.groupby("city")["delivery_time_minutes"].agg(["mean", "sum"])` computes both in one call.

steps.title: Turning a wide table into a long one with melt()
steps.lede: A wide summary table has one column per month. melt() unpivots those columns into rows — one row per city-month combination.

blocks.text: The SwiftDrop monthly deliveries table has one row per city and separate columns `jan_deliveries`, `feb_deliveries`, `mar_deliveries`. Many analysis tools and visualisation libraries expect one row per city-month combination instead — that's the long format.

`melt()` reshapes a DataFrame from wide to long format: the columns listed as `id_vars` stay as identifier columns, while all other columns are unpivoted into two new columns — one holding the original column names and one holding their values. `city_deliveries.melt(id_vars=["city"])` keeps `city` as an identifier and turns the three month columns into two new columns.

The default output column names are `variable` and `value`. Use `var_name` and `value_name` to rename them: `city_deliveries.melt(id_vars=["city"], var_name="month", value_name="deliveries")` gives the two new columns clearer names.

after.caption: Long format — one row per city-month, month column renamed via var_name='month'

blocks.change_summary: Wide table (3 rows × 4 columns) melted to long format (9 rows × 3 columns) with id_vars=['city'], var_name='month', value_name='deliveries'.

steps.title: Groupby aggregation and melt — key takeaways
steps.lede: groupby summarises data by group; melt reshapes wide tables into the long format that analysis tools commonly expect.

blocks.text: Split, apply, combine is the whole idea — `groupby` gives you one call that does all three steps for whatever key and aggregation you choose. Chain `.mean()`, `.sum()`, or `.agg([...])` after `groupby(key)` to get per-group summaries; the group keys become the result's index by default. `melt()` is the complementary reshape: it unpivots wide columns into rows, keeping `id_vars` fixed and turning the rest into a `variable`/`value` pair that you can rename with `var_name` and `value_name`.

remediation_steps.lede: groupby always does the same three things: split the rows into groups, apply a function to each group, then combine the results.

blocks.text: **Group by** refers to a process involving one or more of the following steps: splitting the data into groups based on some criteria, applying a function to each group independently, and combining the results into a data structure. For SwiftDrop orders: split every order into its city's group, apply "average delivery time" within each group, then combine the per-city averages into one summary table.

remediation_steps.title: Renaming the variable and value columns in melt()
remediation_steps.lede: melt() always produces two new columns. By default they're called 'variable' and 'value' — var_name and value_name let you rename them.

blocks.text: The default `variable` and `value` column names produced by `melt()` can be renamed using its `var_name` and `value_name` parameters. Passing `var_name="month"` renames the column that holds the original column names; passing `value_name="deliveries"` renames the column that holds their values.

    id_vars=['city'],
    var_name='month',
    value_name='deliveries'
)

steps.title: Stacking DataFrames with pd.concat()
steps.lede: January, February, and March orders each live in their own table. pd.concat() glues them into one combined DataFrame in a single call.

blocks.text: `pd.concat()` concatenates multiple Series or DataFrame objects along an axis. Pass a list of DataFrames: `pd.concat([jan_orders, feb_orders, mar_orders])`. By default it stacks them **row-wise**, appending each one's rows below the previous — so the result has every January row, then every February row, then every March row, one after another.

`pd.concat()` takes an `axis` parameter. By default (no `axis` argument) it stacks row-wise. Passing `axis=1` places the DataFrames side by side as columns: `pd.concat([orders_basic_info, orders_extra_columns], axis=1)` lines the two tables up next to each other, column by column.

after.code:
all_orders = pd.concat([jan_orders, feb_orders, mar_orders])
print(all_orders.shape)  # (15, 5)
print(all_orders.head())

annotations.text: Three same-column tables stacked row-wise
15 rows = 5 Jan + 5 Feb + 5 Mar

steps.title: Joining two DataFrames on a shared key with merge()
steps.lede: Orders and driver details live in separate tables, linked by driver_id. merge() matches rows on that shared key and combines the columns.

blocks.text: `merge()` combines two DataFrames by matching values in a shared key column, specified with the `on` parameter: `orders.merge(drivers, on="driver_id")`. The result contains one row for every matched pair — columns from both tables side by side.

The `how` parameter controls which keys are kept. `how='inner'` (the default) keeps only key values present in **both** DataFrames — a `driver_id` that appears in orders but not in drivers won't survive an inner merge, and vice versa.

When a key value does not appear in one of the two DataFrames, the corresponding values contributed by that DataFrame in the joined result are `NA`. This is what happens once a join type other than the default inner merge is used and unmatched keys are allowed to stay in the result.

Unmatched keys in the result get NA values from the missing side.

steps.title: Left, right, and outer joins
steps.lede: Beyond the default inner join, three other how= values let you keep unmatched rows from one or both sides.

blocks.text: The `how` parameter also accepts `'left'` (keep all keys from the left DataFrame only), `'right'` (keep all keys from the right DataFrame only), and `'outer'` (keep the union of keys from both DataFrames). `orders.merge(drivers, on="driver_id", how="left")` keeps every order, filling in `NA` for driver details on any `driver_id` that merge can't find in the drivers table.

steps.title: Concatenation and merging — key takeaways
steps.lede: concat glues tables end to end; merge matches rows on a shared key. The axis and how parameters control the direction and which rows survive.

blocks.text: `pd.concat()` glues tables end to end — the `axis` argument is just which direction: down for more rows (default), sideways for more columns. `merge()` matches rows on a shared key; setting `how` decides whether unmatched rows on either side get dropped (`inner`) or kept with `NA` gaps (`left`, `right`, `outer`). Use concat when tables share the same columns; use merge when they share a key column.

remediation_steps.lede: axis=0 stacks rows; axis=1 places tables side by side as columns.

blocks.text: `pd.concat()` takes an `axis` parameter: by default (no `axis` argument) it stacks the objects row-wise, while `axis=1` places them side by side as columns. Think of it as which direction "end to end" points — down for more rows, sideways for more columns.

remediation_steps.title: Merging on a key and controlling which rows survive
remediation_steps.lede: merge() matches rows on a shared column. The how= parameter decides whether unmatched rows are dropped or kept with NA.

blocks.text: `merge()` combines two DataFrames by matching values in a shared key column specified with `on`. The `how` parameter controls which keys are kept: `how='inner'` (the default) keeps only key values present in both DataFrames. `how='left'` keeps all keys from the left DataFrame, filling `NA` for any driver details that can't be found in the right table.

# Inner merge — only matched driver_ids survive
result = orders.merge(drivers, on='driver_id')
# driver_id 204 (in drivers but not orders) is dropped

annotations.text: how='inner' is the default — unmatched keys dropped

result = orders.merge(drivers, on='driver_id', how='left')
# Every order row is present; driver_name is NA if driver_id not in drivers

annotations.text: how='left' keeps all left rows; fills NA on right side

blocks.change_summary: Inner merge drops unmatched keys; left merge keeps all left rows and fills NA for missing right-side values.

remediation_steps.title: Why unmatched keys produce NA values
remediation_steps.lede: When a key value exists on only one side of a merge, the columns from the missing side have nothing to contribute — so they become NA.

blocks.text: If a key value does not appear in one of the two DataFrames being merged, the corresponding values contributed by that DataFrame in the joined result are `NA`. This is what happens once a join type other than the default inner merge is used and unmatched keys are allowed to stay in the result — for example, a `driver_id` that exists in orders but not in drivers will have `NA` in every driver column.

tiles.title: Pivot Tables and Exporting to CSV

steps.title: Spreading long data into a wide grid with pivot_table()
steps.lede: The long deliveries table has one row per city-month. pivot_table() spreads it back into a wide grid — cities as rows, months as columns — and handles duplicate cells automatically.

blocks.text: `pivot_table()` reshapes data by turning the distinct values of one column into new columns. Unlike plain `pivot()`, it can handle duplicate index/column combinations by aggregating the numeric values — so it won't raise an error if two rows share the same city and month.

`pivot_table()` takes `index`, `columns`, and `values` arguments: `index` sets the rows of the output table, `columns` sets the new columns, and `values` selects which column to aggregate. `long_deliveries.pivot_table(index="city", columns="month", values="deliveries")` puts each city on its own row, each month as its own column, and the delivery counts as the values filling the grid.

before.caption: long_deliveries — one row per city-month combination

after.code:
wide = long_deliveries.pivot_table(
    index='city',
    columns='month',
    values='deliveries'
)
print(wide)

annotations.text: index='city' → cities become rows
columns='month' → month values become column headers
values='deliveries' → delivery counts fill the grid

blocks.change_summary: Long table (8 rows × 3 columns) pivoted to wide format (3 rows × 3 month columns) with city as index.

steps.title: Controlling how duplicate cells are combined with aggfunc
steps.lede: When two rows share the same index and column values, pivot_table() must combine them. aggfunc controls how.

blocks.text: `pivot_table()` combines rows that share the same index/column values using `aggfunc`, which defaults to `'mean'`. Passing `aggfunc='sum'` (or another function) changes how those values are combined — so if a city had two rows for the same month, the default call would average them instead of erroring, and adding `aggfunc='sum'` would total them instead.

steps.title: Writing a DataFrame to a CSV file with to_csv()
steps.lede: Once the data is clean and shaped, to_csv() writes it to a file. One argument controls whether the row index is included.

blocks.text: The `to_csv()` method on a Series or DataFrame writes its contents to a CSV file; the destination path or buffer is its only required argument: `orders.to_csv("cleaned_orders.csv")` writes the full orders table to a file.

`to_csv()`'s `index` argument controls whether the row labels are written to the file; it defaults to `True`. Passing `index=False` omits them: `orders.to_csv("cleaned_orders.csv", index=False)` writes the same file without an extra index column at the start.

orders.to_csv('cleaned_orders.csv', index=False)
# CSV has no extra column:
# order_id,city,delivery_time_minutes,...
# 1001,Lagos,18,...

annotations.text: No leading comma — index omitted from file

steps.lede: pivot_table() spreads long data into a wide grid and handles duplicates; to_csv() writes the result to a file.

blocks.text: `pivot_table()` spreads long data wider by turning one column's values into new column headers, aggregating whenever more than one row lands in the same cell. Pass `index`, `columns`, and `values` to define the shape; use `aggfunc='sum'` (or another function) to control how duplicates are combined. Once the table is ready, `to_csv(path)` writes it to a file — add `index=False` to omit the row labels from the output.

remediation_steps.title: How aggfunc controls duplicate cell values in pivot_table()
remediation_steps.lede: When two rows share the same index and column values, pivot_table() must combine them. aggfunc tells it how.

blocks.text: `pivot_table()` combines rows that share the same index/column values using `aggfunc`, which defaults to `'mean'`. Passing `aggfunc='sum'` changes how those values are combined — so if a city had two rows for the same month, the default call would average them instead of erroring, and adding `aggfunc='sum'` would total them instead.

before.code:
# Default aggfunc='mean'
wide = long_deliveries.pivot_table(
    index='city', columns='month', values='deliveries'
)
# Duplicate city-month rows are averaged

annotations.text: aggfunc='mean' is the default — duplicates averaged

after.code:
# aggfunc='sum' totals duplicate rows instead
wide = long_deliveries.pivot_table(
    index='city', columns='month', values='deliveries',
    aggfunc='sum'
)
# Duplicate city-month rows are summed

annotations.text: aggfunc='sum' → duplicates totalled, not averaged

blocks.change_summary: Default aggfunc='mean' averages duplicate cells; aggfunc='sum' totals them instead.

remediation_steps.title: The index argument in to_csv()
remediation_steps.lede: By default to_csv() writes the row index as an extra column. index=False omits it.

blocks.text: `to_csv()`'s `index` argument controls whether the row (index) labels are written to the file; it defaults to `True`, and passing `index=False` omits them. When the index is just a default integer range (0, 1, 2, …), it adds an unnamed column to the CSV that most downstream tools don't expect — `index=False` prevents that.

before.code:
# index=True (default) — row labels written to file
orders.to_csv('cleaned_orders.csv')
# First column in file: 0, 1, 2, ... (the index)

annotations.text: Extra unnamed column — the DataFrame's row index

after.code:
# index=False — row labels omitted
orders.to_csv('cleaned_orders.csv', index=False)
# File starts directly with order_id, city, ...

annotations.text: No extra column — cleaner output for downstream tools

blocks.change_summary: index=True (default) writes row labels as an extra column; index=False omits them.
